title: Fitbit Air Is a Data Play With a Strap
description: The Fitbit Air is a $99.99 screenless band with a $100-a-year coach. I wore it. My RingConn already does the job, and I'm still hunting for a sensor I can't feel.

title: The Box Under the Desk
description: Every serious AI deployment in a hospital hits the same wall: where does the data go. A Dell Pro Max with GB10 sitting in a clinic doesn't have that problem.

title: My medical record lives on a GB10 now
The Algorithm Will See You Now
Can AI restore humanity in healthcare?
description: Ten years. That's how long it took doctors to find my diagnosis.

title: Patient voices in Digital Health products
description: There's a pattern in digital health that I've watched repeat itself for a decade.

title: The Entrepreneurial Body Keeps the Score: What Building a Business with Chronic Illness Really Looks Like
description: Mid-pitch, performing confidence while your body is screaming to stop, genuinely unsure if it'll cooperate for the next five hours. That's the reality startup culture doesn't talk about.

title: We need more patient voices in MedTech
The skills nobody taught me to name
description: I want to name something that chronically ill people do every day and never put on a CV.

title: Machines handle information. Humans handle transformation.
description: It took me almost a decade to get diagnosed.

title: Health IT is broken, Let's fix it.
description: Nurses buried in data entry, doctors transcribing instead of treating, patients repeating their history at every login. Health IT doesn't need another app. It needs one shared standard.

title: Why disabled & chronically ill people are your best employees
description: I built eight organisations from my bed.

title: Unlocking the Superpowers of Necessity: Why Chronically Ill and Disabled People May Be Our Best Employees
description: As an entrepreneur living with chronic pain, I've watched limitation get mistaken for weakness. It's usually the opposite: constraint is what built the skills employers actually need.

title: Is it Our Job to State Our Disabilities?
description: Imagine everyone carries an invisible backpack. Some carry a kilo, some ten. You can't tell by looking. That's what life with invisible illness is like, and it raises a real question: whose job is it to name it?
